claims.text: New product development is the work a business does to create a product new to its range or new to its market, whether an improved version of an existing product or a product it has never sold before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Developing a new product tends to benefit a business by refreshing its range and giving customers a new reason to buy, because tastes and fashions change and a static range loses attention.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: New product development carries real limitations: development costs are paid before any revenue arrives, and demand for a new product is unproven, so the product can fail and the money spent is not recovered.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A successful new product can differentiate a business from its rivals, because buyers who want what the new product does have a reason to choose that business rather than a competitor.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Brand image is the set of ideas, feelings and expectations customers hold about a product or business - the reputation attached to the name in the customer's mind.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A recognised and trusted brand image tends to raise sales, because a known name lowers the risk a buyer feels at the moment of choice, making the purchase quicker and more comfortable.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Brand image builds customer loyalty: buyers who were satisfied re-choose the name they trust, and loyal buyers tend to be less drawn away by a rival's lower price, because they weigh quality and habit against small price gaps.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Building a brand image costs money and time - consistent quality, promotion and packaging over years - and one widely-shared failure can damage it, so the image is an asset the business keeps maintaining.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Packaging is the material that contains and protects a product - the wrapper, box, bottle or packet the product is sold in.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Packaging plays a role beyond protection: it carries information such as contents and weight, presents the brand name at the point of sale, and can persuade the customer, because the pack is often the closest advertisement the product has.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Packaging choices face limits: better packs cost more per unit, and wasted packaging can put environmentally-conscious customers off, so the gain in sales must be weighed against the cost and the waste.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The product life cycle is the pattern of sales a product passes through from its development to its final withdrawal, drawn as a curve of sales against time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main stages of the product life cycle are development, where the product is designed and tested; introduction, where sales begin slowly at a launch price; growth, where sales rise quickly as awareness spreads; maturity, where sales flatten because most willing buyers already have it; and decline, where sales fall as tastes and technology move on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Extension strategies are actions taken at maturity to push decline further away, such as updated versions, new packaging, new markets or market segments, and price promotions on the established product.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An extension strategy can delay decline because a familiar product given a fresh reason to buy recovers attention, but the development and promotion it needs are paid up front, so a strategy that customers reject can spend money speeding the decline it was meant to delay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The marketing mix is the combination of decisions a business makes about product, price, place and promotion, combined to sell the product to its target customers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The stage a product has reached in its life cycle influences marketing decisions: at introduction, promotion informs and the price is set either high to skim from early buyers or low to penetrate quickly, while at maturity promotion shifts to reminders and loyalty and pricing turns competitive, because awareness is already built and rivals are closest.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Reading the stage correctly matters because decisions suited to one stage fit another badly: launch-scale spending on a declining product wastes money, and cutting the price of a growing product gives away margin the demand would have carried.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost-plus pricing sets the price by working out the full cost of one unit and adding a percentage mark-up on top of that cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Competitive pricing sets the price at or near the level rivals charge for similar products, because buyers can see the going rate and compare.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Penetration pricing sets a deliberately low launch price to win market share quickly and to leave rivals little margin to chase.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price skimming sets a high launch price for a new product with no direct rival, taking a high margin from the customers who want to be first, with the price typically reduced later as competition arrives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotional pricing offers a temporary price reduction - a money-off week, a two-for-one offer - to lift sales for a short period rather than changing the standing price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The pricing methods carry benefits and limitations: cost-plus covers costs but ignores what customers will pay; competitive pricing matches the market but can starve a high-cost business of margin; penetration wins share but makes a later price rise hard; skimming earns from early buyers but invites rivals in; promotional pricing lifts sales briefly but trains buyers to wait for offers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price is the amount of money a customer is asked to pay for one unit of a product; of the four marketing mix elements, it is the one that brings revenue in rather than costing the business money.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choosing a pricing method means fitting the method to the circumstances - what the product's costs are, how many rivals sell close substitutes, how new the product is, and how strong the brand is - because the right price depends on facts about the market, not on the business's preference.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Demand for a product is price elastic when the quantity demanded responds more strongly than the price change that caused it, so a small price rise can lose a large share of sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Demand is price inelastic when the quantity demanded responds less strongly than the price change, so a price rise loses few sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The responsiveness of demand matters in pricing decisions: raising the price of a product whose demand is price inelastic tends to raise revenue, because sales barely fall, while raising the price of a product whose demand is price elastic tends to reduce revenue, because the sales lost outweigh the higher price each remaining sale earns.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A distribution channel is the route a product takes from the business that makes it to the final consumer - for example producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer, or producer direct to the consumer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each channel has advantages and disadvantages: a wholesaler buys in bulk and stores stock, sparing the producer transport and storage, but takes a share of the final price; a retailer reaches customers where they shop, but chooses which products to stock; selling direct keeps the whole price and the customer relationship, but the business carries the delivery, storage and selling work itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Perishable and fragile products suit short, fast channels, while long channels suit low-value products sold in many small outlets, because each extra stage adds handling and time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Direct-to-consumer selling means the producer sells straight to the final customer with no wholesaler or retailer between them, through its own shop, market stall, website or delivery round.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choosing a distribution channel means fitting it to the circumstances - what the product is, where the customers are, and what size the business is - because a channel the business cannot operate or afford does not reach customers no matter how good the product is.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selling direct tends to earn the business a higher margin per unit, because no intermediary takes a share of the price, but the business then carries the storage, delivery and selling work the intermediary would have done.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotion is the communication a business uses to make customers aware of a product and to persuade them to buy it, covering advertising, sales promotion and the messages a business sends about its products.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The aims of promotion differ with the situation: a new business needs awareness first, because customers cannot buy from a business they have not heard of, while an established business defends the buying habits of its existing customers, because keeping a customer costs less than winning one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising is paid promotion through a medium the business does not own - radio, print, posters, television or online placements - carrying a message to customers without a salesperson present.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising influences sales by building awareness and familiarity, because a name a buyer recognises feels less risky to try, and a message that gives a reason to buy can move the buyer to a first purchase.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising has limitations: its costs are paid before any revenue arrives, its effect on sales is hard to measure, and repeated messages are needed because a single exposure is soon forgotten.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sales promotion - short-term offers such as money-off vouchers, free samples and competitions - influences sales by lowering the cost of trying, which wins quick trial and a temporary lift in sales, but the lift fades when the offer ends and buyers can be trained to wait for offers rather than buy at the standing price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost-effectiveness in promotion spending means comparing what each promotion costs with the result it produces, so that the money spent brings in more than it cost and the best option is the one with the strongest result for its price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A promotion budget spent without measuring results can squeeze profit, because the money leaves whether or not the promotion is working, while measuring the cost of each option per new customer lets the business move the budget towards what works.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: E-commerce is buying and selling goods or services over the internet, with orders placed and paid for online and the product delivered or provided digitally.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An e-commerce operation has features of its own: a website or app showing products and prices, online ordering with payment taken there, order confirmation, and delivery or digital supply, running around the clock wherever the customer has a connection.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: E-commerce opens opportunities: a business can sell outside its home town around the clock without opening shops, reach scattered specialist buyers in one place, and gather data on what customers look at; consumers gain wider choice, easier price comparison and shopping from home.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: E-commerce also brings threats: online rivals can reach a town shop's own customers at lower cost, price comparison can pull buyers to the cheapest listing, delivery costs and returns eat margin, and customers cannot touch or try the product before paying.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Social media promotion is the use of platforms where people share posts, pictures and short messages to present a product where followers see it, respond and pass it on to their own contacts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promoting through social media and the internet can cost less than paid advertising per customer reached, because each follower who shares a post carries the message to contacts the business did not pay to reach, and a share arrives with a recommendation's trust attached; the approach needs regular, worth-sharing content, because a silent or dull feed loses followers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price and cost are different figures: price is what the customer pays the business, while cost is what the business pays to make and sell one unit, so a price set below cost loses money on each sale.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price skimming and low or competitive pricing point in opposite directions: skimming sets a launch price above the going rate for a new product with no close rival, while penetration pricing sets a launch price below the going rate and competitive pricing sets the price at or near it; where the launch price sits against rivals' prices, and whether close rivals exist, tells them apart.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Penetration pricing and competitive pricing differ in level, aim and timing: penetration sets a launch price below the going rate to win market share quickly and is usually raised later, while competitive pricing matches the going rate as a standing policy so the price stays inside the range buyers expect.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotional pricing is a pricing method that temporarily cuts the price the customer pays for a unit, while a sales promotion such as a competition or a free gift is a form of promotion that adds an incentive and leaves the price unchanged; whether the price paid for one unit falls tells them apart.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising and sales promotion are often used together but are different forms of promotion: advertising is the paid message carried in a medium, while sales promotion is the short-term offer itself, so an advertisement that announces an offer is advertising carrying a sales promotion; whether the activity is the message or the offer tells them apart.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
